explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. David says, "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want" (Psalm 23:1). In the Bible, "shall not want" means he will never go without what he needs. It is like walking into my bakery when the ovens are warm and the cookie boxes are stacked to the ceiling: nothing is missing.

Not earn, friend. A sheep doesn't punch a clock to get its grass. David says, "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want" (Psalm 23:1), and "want" here means to lack something. With the LORD watching over him, David isn't missing a thing he needs.

Close, baker, but the word here is lack. David writes, "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want" (Psalm 23:1). "Want" is an older way of saying you don't have what you need. Because the LORD is his shepherd, David says he won't go without.

That's the picture right there. David says, "He makes me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside quiet waters" (Psalm 23:2). Sheep don't lie down when they're rattled, and rushing water is hard to drink from. Everything in this verse is calm, settled, and cared for.

Take a look at what the sheep is doing in Psalm 23:2: lying down! David says the LORD makes him lie down in green pastures and leads him beside quiet waters. Nobody is sprinting or grinding here. It is a picture of rest and peace, with the shepherd handling the leading.

The dark valley comes later in the psalm, friend, not here. In Psalm 23:2, David is lying down in green pastures and walking beside quiet waters. When I hear "lie down in green pastures," my whole gold base wants to take a nap. That is pure rest and peace.

Right on the money, baker. David says, "He restores my soul" (Psalm 23:3). Think about how a worn-out stamp gets its sharp edges back so it can press dough again. That is what the LORD does for David on the inside, bringing his soul back to life.

Other scriptures do talk about the LORD testing hearts, like Psalm 17:3, where David says God has tested him. Right here in Psalm 23:3, though, the shepherd is caring for a tired sheep. David says, "He restores my soul," bringing him back when he is worn down.

Proverbs 16:2 says the LORD weighs the motives, so that is a real Bible idea, friend. Here in Psalm 23:3, though, David is still talking about his shepherd's care. He says, "He restores my soul," refreshing him deep down.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His name
explanations.explanation: You nailed it, friend. David says, "He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name" (Psalm 23:3). A shepherd's reputation is tied to how he leads his sheep. The LORD leads David the right way because of who the LORD is.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His flock
explanations.explanation: The flock definitely gets the blessing, baker, so I see why that sounded good. But look at how David finishes the line in Psalm 23:3: "He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name." The LORD puts His own name on the line in how He leads.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His land
explanations.explanation: Not the land on this one, friend. Psalm 23:3 doesn't mention Israel's borders or soil at all. David says the LORD guides him in the paths of righteousness "for the sake of His name." It comes right back to who the Shepherd is.

explanations.answer: Because the LORD is with him
explanations.explanation: That is the whole reason right there. David says to the LORD, "I will fear no evil, for You are with me" (Psalm 23:4). Notice how David goes from talking ABOUT the LORD to talking straight TO Him when the road gets dark. When you are in the shadow, you don't make a speech about your shepherd, you look right at Him.

Friend, a sheep by itself in a dark canyon is not toughing anything out. David doesn't brag on his own grit in Psalm 23:4. He tells the LORD, "I will fear no evil, for You are with me." It is the Shepherd's company that takes the fear away.

David never says how long that valley is, baker. For all we know from Psalm 23:4, it is a long walk through the dark. What changes things for David isn't the size of the valley, it is who is walking beside him: "I will fear no evil, for You are with me."

True indeed, baker. David tells the LORD, "Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me" (Psalm 23:4). A shepherd used those tools to fight off wild animals and to guide the sheep back onto the path. Seeing your shepherd carrying the gear to protect and guide you is a mighty fine sight in the dark.

They really do comfort him, friend! In Psalm 23:4, David says to the LORD, "Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me." Those weren't there to scare the sheep. They were the tools a shepherd used to keep dangers away and keep his flock safe on the trail.

Pull up a chair, baker! David tells the LORD, "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies" (Psalm 23:5). That is a full sit-down meal laid out by the host Himself. If somebody sets out a whole spread for you while trouble is watching, you know the host has everything under control.

A tent fits the outdoor feel of the psalm, and Psalm 27:5 does talk about the LORD hiding David in His tent. Right here in Psalm 23:5, though, the LORD is setting out a meal: "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies." He is welcoming David to sit and eat.

David already did his lying down back in the green pastures in Psalm 23:2! By Psalm 23:5, it is time to eat. David says to the LORD, "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies." The LORD is hosting a meal for him.

Hold the mixer, friend, look closer at where those enemies are! David says in Psalm 23:5, "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies." They aren't miles away, they are right there watching! And David still gets to sit down and eat in peace because the LORD is the one hosting.

You caught it, baker. David says the LORD prepares that table "in the presence of my enemies" (Psalm 23:5). Can you imagine your enemies standing there watching while the LORD sets a feast right in front of you? They can look all they want, because they can't touch a guest at the LORD's table.

That is it, friend. When David says, "my cup overflows" in Psalm 23:5, it links right back to "I shall not want" in verse 1. The LORD doesn't measure His kindness out to the halfway line and stop. He pours until it runs right over the brim.

Now, when I spill chocolate chips all over my apron, that is me getting carried away with the scoop. In Psalm 23:5, though, "my cup overflows" isn't an accident by a clumsy guest. The LORD is the host doing the pouring, and it shows He gives David more than enough.

Nobody is getting hurried out the door at this table, baker. The LORD has prepared the table and anointed David's head with oil (Psalm 23:5), which is how you treat an honored guest who is staying a while. When David says, "my cup overflows," it means the LORD is pouring out more than enough.

Spot on, baker. David says, "Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life" (Psalm 23:6). Notice what is behind him now. Even with enemies around in verse 5, the things actually sticking with David every day of his life are the LORD's goodness and mercy.

God did give wealth and honor to David's son Solomon later on (1 Kings 3:13), and David himself died full of riches and honor (1 Chronicles 29:28). In this song, though, David names something else entirely. Psalm 23:6 says, "Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life."

Those are wonderful gifts from God, friend, and the Bible talks about them plenty. Right here at the end of his shepherd song, though, David is looking at the LORD's kind care chasing after him. He says, "Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life" (Psalm 23:6).

explanations.answer: In the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: What a way to finish the song, friend. David says, "and I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever" (Psalm 23:6). The psalm started out in the open pastures with a shepherd, and it ends at home in the LORD's own house for good. Once the LORD brings you in, you are home.

David did reign as king in Hebron for seven and a half years (2 Samuel 5:5), so you know your David history, baker! But he didn't stay in Hebron forever. At the close of Psalm 23:6, he looks to a much bigger home: "and I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever."

Canaan was the land God promised to Abraham's family (Genesis 17:8), where David lived. Here in Psalm 23:6, though, David makes it personal: he wants to be where the Host is. He finishes by saying, "and I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever."
